en: Seeing their ravines, she wept.
Where they caught foals and tethered mares,
When she saw the place where they had stayed,
Slaughtering colts suckled by barren mares,
When she saw the place where they had lived,
Then your mother Kanykei—
From her precious eyes, like a quail’s,
Tears flowed in separate streams.
From her precious eyes, like black currants,
Tears streamed a whip’s length.
Naming her places, she cried aloud;
Your mother wept and sobbed.
When placed on a blue tile
Breathless in the green valley,
They had been encamped.
When your father lived in happiness,
When their happiness was intact,
When they received whatever they wished,
Cutting strips of otter skin,
When they trimmed their trouser cuffs,
The many Argyn and Kyrgyz people
Were encamped there.
Laughter by day, play by night—
Such were those days.
A dear land of unequaled happiness,
Our people utterly vanished.
At the shoulder of a gray mountain,
On that rugged promontory,
Your leopard elder Bakai’s
Moinok-Tash, where he stood watch—
If you looked toward its steep bank,
Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled there.
This very day in Talas,
Not a Kyrgyz, not even a stump remains;
My heart boils like embers!
That gray round hill, that little pass—
Your father with his forty warriors
Gathered there.
Drawing a line forty foot-lengths around,
They played merry ordo there.
Forty fat mares
They tethered in the middle;
The winners slaughtered them there.
Trampled bare, with nothing left,
This place now lies deserted.
Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled,
Maintaining a court, ruling the people—
So we used to live, dear souls.
Along this Talas,
What is there, and what is gone?
Seeing the empty land without its people,
My heart grieves, my breast burns.
The vain world rose before my eyes.
Your mother has seen much;
I, wretched one, have no regrets.
When those people dwelt here,
Old women chewed fat tails;
Poor men drove a thousand sheep.
Not a young bride lacked happiness.
Not dying with that happiness,
Your mother’s misery boiled over.
Within my breast, my foal,
There is a wound that will not heal.
If I go on telling, my foal,
There are many, many wonders.
My brow bone was curved;
When your father died,
My livelihood proved scant.
The hair upon my brow was grass;
Beyond my good fortune, my suffering,
After your leopard father died,
Was greater by a spear’s length.
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
When many people lay at ease,
When my abundance was intact,
Overwhelming, conquering monsters,
Not mending the companions’ torn clothes,
Having no regard for God,
You never pulled back the smoke-hole cover,
Never eating food left overnight,
That wretched woman who thought herself grand—
Her arrogance fell upon her own head.
She lost her bloodthirsty hero
At thirty-two years of age.
Below, the steep bank and broad valley—
That is the place called Keng-Shor.
Along this very Keng-Shor,
I was the one bereaved of your father Manas!
When the debt fell due,
When death lay in wait,
His eyes barely open, their gaze wandering,
His fine mustache lying smooth,
When your father went to Judgment,
My black hair untouched by a comb,
Here in Keng-Shor itself,
I seized and tore out strand by strand!
Where the strands of my hair fell,
Willows grew, a forest of willows.
The dark tears flowing from my eyes,
Here in Keng-Shor to this day,
Became pools of dark water.
My fierce hero had been a banner for the people.
The dark blood flowing from my face,
Here in Keng-Shor to this day,
Became red stone a horse’s shin high,
Your father had been the people’s leader.
‘If I bury your father openly,
Of those stubborn foes who fought him,
One will dig him up,
And give him to dogs to tear apart,’ I thought.
Without showing a single person,
Without letting a single person know,
I contrived an extraordinary spectacle.
I startled those who saw it.
Your father’s funeral prayer
I had recited without showing him to the people.
Koshoi and Töshtük saw him;
Alas, Khan Bakai saw him.
Careful feeding.
At the place where your father was washed,
Plane trees grew like an enclosure;
The holy khojas gave their aid.
Where he was taken for the funeral prayer,
Abundant plane trees grew;
The Creator Himself gave His aid.
Twisting their mustaches,
The Mustafas gave their aid.
Twisting their beards,
The Mustafas gave their aid.
Your father was a lion for the people.
A fierce hero like him,
Created and brought into being,
Will not be given again soon.
Forty champions who came from Arabia,
Whose speech could not be understood—
I set them to that extraordinary task;
I had them lift and carry him.
Kökbörü and Töshtük were there;
Khan Bakai and Koshoi were there too.
Reciting the funeral prayer and profession of faith,
Where they carried him onward,
Red willows grew in a ridge;
The Creator Himself became their helper.
The holy khojas joined together;
Where they escorted him in a circle,
Until they brought him to his resting place,
Abundant red willows grew;
The Creator Himself became their helper.
This is the place called Keng-Shor;
I am the one bereaved of your father!”
They properly saddled the horses;
The saintly heroes
Recited the Koran for him.
The past came into her mind;
Kanykei wept in desolation.
Allah’s sun in heaven clouded over;
Sixty worries fell upon her together!
The place where she had lived appeared;
Tears poured from her eyes.
Fierce Manas, the leopard,
Seemed to have only just died!
Below Tört-Kül,
To the garden planted by Lord Manas,
Kanykei now came,
And stopped once more.
“See that great mound there—
Your father’s great mosque.
They felled all its willows,
Demolished all its walls,
Pulled out its pillars.
Waging war upon a mosque,
But God took that vile man.
When your father was alive,
This great mosque standing here—
Within the great mosque,
There were lords and khans,
And many exemplary men.
Within that mosque,
Lords had stood, khans had stood.
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels—
These were the scoundrels' deeds:
They cast down all the thrones;
They demolished all the buildings.
They pulled out the pillars;
The great mosque was destroyed
And left level with the ground.
Its hollows filled up;
It became a mound like Tört-Kül.
My warrior lord, may you not die;
May your poor soul never see such torment!”
Seeing her land, she grew distraught;
Your mother wept in anguish.
Blood ran from her black eyes;
How bitterly she sobbed!
Those who stood watching
Had their hearts grievously stirred.
Your mother wept and shook;
What could poor Chiyirdi do?
Like a twig put in water,
She swayed, wailing and weeping.
“My orphan, whom I cherish,
If I tell you of the old days,
You will think I am boasting.
Sixty thousand horses in the hills,
Fine steeds and coursers mingled.
What power have I against God?
My support behind me, my son, was young.
Bereft of composure and support,
Our poor heads were troubled.
Then all our elder and younger kinsmen were foes!
From wounded honor I wished to die,
Yet I remained alive and did not die,
My dear child, because you were there.
From wounded honor I wished to depart,
Yet I did not depart then,
Because my needed orphan was there!
If I died of anguish,
My cherished orphan
Would be like an extinguished fire, I thought.
So I spared my life;
I did not spill my blood.
Here along the Talas,
Living among the Argyn,
With my young child beneath my arm,
I suffered humiliation and hardship;
Then my poor soul was thrown into turmoil.
Allah's sun in the sky grew overcast;
Sixty troubles came upon my head at once.
His father's countless treasures and great wealth—
Those dogs will plunder them, I thought.
When the orphan returns,
He will have no wealth at all
And be left powerless, I thought.
God may take me thus, I thought.
There is a place where I hid your treasure.
I, your unfortunate mother,
Have a tale that does not end.
Without letting a single person know,
Without a single person sensing it,
There at gray-mottled Kyzyl-Too,
I devised this arduous undertaking.
From the Argyn and the Kyrgyz
I took five strong men.
I gave horses as their wages.
Besides their wages,
I promptly gave gold and silver.
I let them crunch sugar like snow;
I let them drink their fill of black tea.
Spending my livestock,
I implored the five strong men.
I gave sharp tools of solid iron;
I gave steel mattocks as equipment.
I had them dig into the gray cliff face.
All the treasure
I entrusted to their keeping.
I had the opening carefully hollowed out,
